title: Merge two metadata trees
label: idb
statement:
Merge two trees containing:

• key
• value

The value represents the sum of this node and its child node values.

When merging:

• absent branches are created
• existing branch values are summed
• child ordering is arbitrary
• keys are unique among siblings

Implement:

merge(TreeNode s, TreeNode t)

Follow-ups:
1. Best serialization format and trade-offs
2. Transform result into a side-heavy tree
3. Concurrent merges
4. Same tree used as source by one thread and target by another
5. Very large serialized trees (1GB+)
6. Performance optimization
7. Memory considerations

flaw.ctx: The assistant produced this. Later a user reported: "After merging two config trees, editing the result changed one of the inputs."
flaw.answer: The result reuses `a.Children` — the same dictionary object. Merging adds b's children into **input a**, and editing the result edits a.
flaw.fix: Build new nodes and new collections all the way down (Fixes.D8_Merge).

qa.a: O(1) average for lookup, insert, remove; O(n) worst case if many keys collide. Enumeration is O(n) and order is not guaranteed.

Separate chaining, but without node objects: an `int[] buckets` of indices into an `Entry[]` array, each entry carrying its hash, key, value and a `next` index. Colliding keys form a chain through `next`.

When the entries array is full it grows to a larger prime (about double) and every entry is rehashed into new buckets — O(n) for that insert, amortised O(1). Pre-size with the constructor capacity when you know n.
Removing does not shrink anything: freed slots go on a free list for reuse. `TrimExcess()` shrinks. A struct key that is large is copied into every entry.

Most operators (`Where`, `Select`, `OrderBy`) are deferred: nothing runs until enumeration. `ToList`, `ToArray`, `Count()`, `First`, `Sum` execute immediately. `OrderBy` is deferred but buffers everything when enumerated.
The whole pipeline runs twice — including any I/O behind the source. Materialise once with `ToList()` if you need it twice.
An enumerator per operator, plus delegate and closure allocations for captured variables. Negligible for setup code, measurable in a per-request hot path.

qa.q: When is an explicit loop better?
qa.a: Hot paths, early exit with complex state, mutating as you go, or when you need to state complexity exactly — R5 hid an O(n log n) sort per call inside one readable line.

learn.title: 1 · Problem
learn.md:
> Merge two trees containing:
> 
> • key
> • value
> 
> The value represents the sum of this node and its child node values.
> 
> When merging:
> 
> • absent branches are created
> • existing branch values are summed
> • child ordering is arbitrary
> • keys are unique among siblings
> 
> Implement:
> 
> merge(TreeNode s, TreeNode t)
> 
> Follow-ups:
> 1. Best serialization format and trade-offs
> 2. Transform result into a side-heavy tree
> 3. Concurrent merges
> 4. Same tree used as source by one thread and target by another
> 5. Very large serialized trees (1GB+)
> 6. Performance optimization
> 7. Memory considerations

Two trees describing the same hierarchy, each holding partial totals. Merge them into one tree whose values are the combined totals, creating branches that exist on only one side.

A merged tree. Same shape as the union of the two inputs; values summed where both have a node.

learn.title: 2 · Clarifications
learn.md:
"The value represents the sum of this node and its child node values" is an **invariant**, not just a description, and it has a consequence worth stating: the value is partly derived. A node’s own contribution is `value − sum(children.value)`.

The good news is that the invariant is preserved automatically by summing. If both inputs satisfy `value = own + Σ children`, then adding them gives `(own₁+own₂) + Σ (children₁+children₂)`, which satisfies it too. So **nothing has to be recomputed** — and saying that is better than either silently relying on it or writing a fix-up pass.

What the statement does not say: whether the merge may mutate its inputs, and what to do if the two roots have different keys. I build a new tree and mutate nothing — which is what makes follow-up 4 answerable — and I throw on mismatched roots rather than inventing a parent.

| Assumption | If it is wrong |
|---|---|
| Neither input is mutated; the merge returns a new tree. | The statement does not say. It is what makes `Merge(x, x)` safe and concurrent readers safe, and it is the answer to follow-up 4 — so it is worth choosing deliberately and saying why. |
| Both roots have the same key. | Otherwise there is no single tree to produce. I throw; the alternative is inventing a synthetic parent, which silently changes the data. |
| Values are non-negative and fit in a `long`. | `int` would overflow on a merge of large totals, and the whole point is that values are sums. Negative values would break the `IsConsistent` check but not the merge. |
| Trees are deep enough to matter. | Follow-up 5 says 1 GB, so recursion depth is a real risk and an iterative version has to exist. Assuming shallow trees would make follow-up 5 unanswerable. |

learn.title: 3 · Key insight
learn.md:
Two observations. The first is small and the second is what the follow-ups are built on.

**One: children keyed rather than positional turns the merge into three cases.** At each node, look at every child key on both sides. In both → recurse. Only in `s` → copy the branch. Only in `t` → copy the branch. That is the same three-case shape as merging two sorted lists or comparing two trees, and with a dictionary of children each case is an O(1) probe. LeetCode 617 has the same three cases hidden in its null checks; making the children keyed just makes them explicit.

**Two: build a new tree rather than mutating either input.** This looks like a style choice and it is the load-bearing decision of the whole question, because it answers three of the seven supplied follow-ups at once.

Follow-up 4 asks what happens when one thread uses a tree as a source while another uses it as a target. If the merge mutates the target, the first thread is reading a tree that is changing underneath it — torn reads, double counting, and if the two are the *same* tree, potentially a dictionary being enumerated while it is written, which throws. If the merge only ever reads its inputs, all of that disappears: any number of threads may merge from the same trees simultaneously, and `Merge(x, x)` is well defined.

So: **choose the pure version first and let it answer the concurrency follow-ups**, rather than writing the in-place version and then trying to lock it. The in-place variant is worth keeping to name the trap — which is why `MergeInto` is in the listing and refuses a self-merge explicitly.

And the invariant needs no maintenance, because summation is additive. That is worth noticing rather than defending: if the invariant had been "value is the *maximum* of this node and its children", merging would have needed a fix-up pass, and this question would be materially harder.

learn.title: 4 · Approach
learn.md:
**Brute force.** Serialise both trees to flat lists of `(path, value)` pairs, merge the lists by path, then rebuild a tree from the merged paths. *O(n log n) for the sort, plus O(n · depth) to build and compare the path strings. O(n) space, with the paths often larger than the trees.*

**Why not good enough.** It works, and it is genuinely how you would do this **out of core** for follow-up 5 — so it is worth stating rather than dismissing. In memory it is strictly worse: it materialises a path string per node, which for a deep tree costs more than the tree, and it pays a sort for an ordering the recursion gets for free. The recursion is O(n) with no sort and no path strings. But keep this approach in your pocket, because it is the external-merge answer.

**The approach.**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| INPUT | Two `MetaNode` roots, each with `Dictionary<string, MetaNode>` children |
| TRANSFORMATION | None. The keyed children are already the index the merge needs. |
| DATA STRUCTURE | `Dictionary<string, MetaNode>` per node for O(1) child lookup |
| ALGORITHM | Recurse in lockstep: sum the values, recurse on shared keys, clone branches present on one side only |
| OUTPUT | A new tree; both inputs untouched |

learn.title: 5 · Why the approach works
learn.md:
- Either side null → return a clone of the other.
- Root keys differ → throw; there is no single tree to produce.
- Create a new node with `s.Value + t.Value`.
- For each child of `s`: present in `t` → recurse; otherwise clone the branch.
- For each child of `t` not already handled → clone the branch.
- Return the new node.

- Children are identified by **key**, not by position. That is the whole difference from LeetCode 617 and it is what makes child lookup a dictionary probe.
- Keys are unique among siblings, so a key identifies at most one child — which is what lets the children be a dictionary at all.
- Child ordering is arbitrary, so the output order carries no meaning. That matters for serialisation, where you have to *choose* an order.
- The value invariant is additive, so summing preserves it.

learn.title: 6 · Data structures
learn.md:
| Structure | Why |
|---|---|
| `Dictionary<string, MetaNode>` for children | Keys are unique among siblings, so a dictionary is the exact model, and "is this key on the other side" becomes O(1). A list of children would make the merge O(c²) per node. |
| `StringComparer.Ordinal` | Keys are identifiers. Culture-aware comparison is both slower and, in the general case, capable of treating distinct keys as equal — which here would merge two different branches into one and silently corrupt the totals. |
| A new tree rather than in-place | The decision that answers follow-ups 3 and 4. Inputs are read-only, so concurrent merges from shared trees need no locking at all. |
| `long` values | The values are sums of sums. `int` overflows, silently and negatively. |
| An iterative variant alongside the recursive one | Follow-up 5 specifies 1 GB trees, and the recursion depth is the height. The iterative version with an explicit stack is the one that survives a 60,000-deep chain — tested. |

learn.title: 7 · C# implementation — walkthrough
learn.md:
**Why `Merge` allocates a new node before looking at any child.** `new MetaNode(s.Key, s.Value + t.Value)` first, then the children are filled in. Nothing reads from the inputs after they have been written to, because they are never written to at all. That is the property the concurrency follow-ups need, and it comes from this line rather than from a lock.

**The two loops, and the `ContainsKey` guard on the second.** The first loop handles "in s" — recursing when `t` also has the key, cloning otherwise. The second handles "only in t", guarded by `!merged.Children.ContainsKey(kv.Key)` so shared keys are not processed twice. Without the guard, a shared child would be overwritten by a clone of `t`’s branch and `s`’s subtree would vanish — with a plausible-looking result.

**`MergeInto` exists to name the trap, not to be used.** It throws on `ReferenceEquals(target, source)`. Self-merging in place double-counts, and worse, it enumerates `source.Children` while writing to `target.Children` — the same dictionary — which throws `InvalidOperationException` at an unpredictable point, leaving the tree half-merged. **This is follow-up 4 in miniature** and it is why the pure version is the answer.

**`MergeIterative` and the work stack of triples.** `Stack<(MetaNode S, MetaNode T, MetaNode Out)>` — the output node is carried alongside the two inputs, so children can be attached without a parent pointer. Tested on a 60,000-deep chain, which the recursive version would not survive. Note that `Clone` is **still recursive**, so a deep branch present on only one side would still overflow — an honest gap, and the fix is an iterative clone.

**`IsConsistent` checks the invariant, and only one direction.** It verifies `value >= sum(children)`, i.e. that a node’s own contribution is non-negative. It cannot verify more without knowing the intended own-values. Writing the invariant as a checkable function is worth doing precisely because the statement gave it as prose — it is the assertion a reviewer would ask for.

**`SideHeavy.Encode` orders siblings before encoding.** `OrderBy(k => k.Key, StringComparer.Ordinal)`. The statement says child ordering is arbitrary, and a dictionary has no order at all — so any serialised or linked form must **choose** one, or two encodings of the same tree will differ. That determinism is what makes the encoding comparable, hashable and diffable, and it is the detail that connects follow-up 2 to follow-up 1.

**`Decode` walks the sibling chain, and the recursion handles the subtree.** `for (child = b.Left; child != null; child = child.Right)` iterates one level; `Decode(child)` handles that child’s own children via `child.Left`. Getting this wrong — recursing in a way that also follows `Right` — duplicates siblings into the wrong level, which is why the round trip is asserted in the tests rather than eyeballed.

learn.title: 8 · Complexity
learn.md:
| Operation | Time | Space | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Merge` | O(nₛ + nₜ) | O(nₛ + nₜ) | Every node of both inputs visited once; the output is a full copy |
| `MergeInto` | O(nₛ + nₜ) | O(nₜ) new nodes only | Reuses the target, so only cloned branches allocate |
| `MergeIterative` | O(nₛ + nₜ) | O(n) heap stack | Same work; the stack moves from the thread stack to the heap |
| `Clone` | O(n) | O(n) | One new node per source node |
| `IsConsistent` | O(n) | O(h) | One pass, recursive |
| `SideHeavy.Encode` | O(n log c) | O(n) | The `log c` is sorting each node’s c children |

**The pure merge allocates a node for every node in both inputs, and that is its real cost — not the time.** For 1 GB trees the copy is the problem, not the traversal: you need roughly 2× the memory of the result live at once. `MergeInto` avoids it by reusing the target, which is exactly the trade the concurrency follow-ups make you choose about. Naming memory rather than time as the binding constraint is the right framing for follow-ups 5 and 7.

learn.title: 9 · Edge cases
learn.md:
| Case | Behaviour |
|---|---|
| Either input null | Returns a clone of the other. A **clone**, not the same reference, so the caller cannot accidentally alias an input into the result. |
| Both null | Returns null. |
| Root keys differ | Throws. Inventing a synthetic parent would change the data silently. |
| `Merge(x, x)` | Safe — values double, `x` untouched. The pure version handles it with no special case. |
| `MergeInto(x, x)` | **Refused explicitly.** Double-counts and can throw mid-merge, leaving the tree half-updated. |
| Deep chain (60,000 nodes) | Recursive merge overflows; `MergeIterative` handles it. Tested. `Clone` is still recursive — a stated gap. |
| One tree a single node | The other’s children are all cloned across. |
| Value overflow | `long`. `int` would wrap negative on large sums. |
| Duplicate sibling keys | Impossible by the stated constraint, and the dictionary enforces it. |
| Empty children on both sides | A leaf whose value is the sum of the two. |

learn.title: 16 · Follow-up questions
learn.md:
**What is the best serialization format, and what are the trade-offs?**

Whatever the format, two problems have to be solved: **key and value per node**, and **where a node’s children end**. Positional null markers (297’s approach) do not work, because the arity is unbounded — so either a child count per node or an explicit terminator.

A length-prefixed binary format is the right answer for size and speed: `[keyLen][key][value][childCount]` then the children, depth-first. JSON is the right answer for debuggability and for crossing a service boundary you do not own. Protobuf sits between and buys schema evolution, which matters if this format outlives the code.

And **sibling order must be canonicalised** — sorted by key — or two serialisations of the same tree differ, which breaks hashing, diffing and any content-addressed cache.

*Trade-off:* Binary is compact and fast and unreadable, and versioning it is on you. JSON is roughly 3–5× larger and parses far slower, and any engineer can debug it with `cat`. For 1 GB trees the size difference is the deciding factor and I would go binary with a version byte; for an API I would take JSON and not think about it again. The canonical ordering is not a trade — it is required either way.

**Transform the result into a side-heavy tree.**

Each node’s `Left` is its first child and its `Right` is its next sibling. Every n-ary tree maps to a binary tree uniquely and reversibly, and the tree leans right by exactly the width of the widest sibling list. Siblings are sorted first, so the encoding is deterministic.

*Trade-off:* The binary form has fixed arity, so it serialises with positional markers and fits any binary-tree algorithm — which is the point. The cost is depth: a node with 1,000 children becomes a right chain of 1,000, so a recursive walk over the encoded form is far deeper than over the original. If the interviewer meant something else by side-heavy — a deliberate imbalance, or all children on one side — I would ask, because the word is not standard and guessing would waste the answer.

**Several threads merge concurrently.**

`Merge` only reads its inputs and only writes nodes it has just allocated, so any number of threads may merge from the same trees with **no synchronisation at all**. Nothing is shared and mutable.

The work also parallelises naturally: each child subtree is independent, so `Parallel.ForEach` over the children of the root, with a depth cutoff so small subtrees are merged inline rather than scheduled.

*Trade-off:* Purity buys lock-free concurrency and costs a full copy. `MergeInto` avoids the copy and immediately needs locking — and locking a tree correctly means either one lock (no concurrency) or per-node locks with a consistent acquisition order (deadlock risk, and hard to review). Parallelising has a real cutoff: below a few thousand nodes the task overhead exceeds the merge, so measure rather than parallelise everything.

**The same tree is used as a source by one thread and as a target by another.**

With `Merge`, there is no target. Nothing is written to either input, so the scenario cannot arise: both threads read, both produce their own result.

With `MergeInto` it is a genuine race, and it is worth being concrete about the damage. The reader sees some children already summed and others not — a torn read, producing a total that corresponds to no point in time. And if the source and target are the same object, a dictionary is enumerated while being written, which throws `InvalidOperationException` partway through and leaves the tree half-merged with no way to roll back.

*Trade-off:* If in-place is unavoidable for memory reasons, the answer is **copy-on-write with an atomic publish**: build the merged tree, then swap the root reference with `Interlocked.Exchange`. Readers hold whichever root they picked up and see a consistent snapshot; there is no locking and no torn read. The cost is that the copy is back, which is the honest circle: you can have immutability or you can have the memory saving, not both.

**The serialized trees are over 1 GB.**

Three things.

**Do not recurse.** `MergeIterative` moves the stack to the heap; it is tested on a 60,000-deep chain. (`Clone` is still recursive — that would need fixing too.)

**Stream instead of materialising.** If both files are written with siblings in canonical key order, the merge is a **single synchronised pass** over the two streams, writing the output as it goes — exactly a sorted-list merge, with O(depth) memory rather than O(n). That is the real answer, and it is why the canonical ordering from follow-up 1 matters here.

**If they are not ordered**, sort externally first, or fall back to the path-keyed external merge from the brute-force section — which is exactly where that approach earns its place.

*Trade-off:* Streaming is O(depth) memory instead of O(n) and needs the inputs canonically ordered, so it pushes a requirement back onto whoever writes the files. It also gives up random access: you cannot answer "what is the value at this path" without a full pass. In .NET there is a further specific: any buffer over 85 KB lands on the **Large Object Heap**, which is not compacted by default, so a 1 GB merge that allocates large arrays fragments the heap. Use pooled buffers and `Span<T>` slices rather than fresh arrays per node.

**Optimise the performance.**

In order of payoff. **Iterate the smaller tree** and probe the larger, so the number of dictionary lookups is bounded by the smaller side. **Pre-size the child dictionaries** to the combined child count, avoiding rehashing as they fill. **Intern or pool the key strings**, since the same keys recur across a large tree and each one is otherwise a separate allocation. **Parallelise across the root’s children** with a size cutoff. And **`StringComparer.Ordinal`**, which is both faster and the correct comparer.

*Trade-off:* The first three are close to free and I would do them without measuring. Parallelism has a real cutoff and can be slower on small trees. String interning trades a permanent table for reduced allocation, which is right for a long-lived service and wrong for a one-off tool. The honest headline is that the merge is **allocation-bound, not compute-bound** — so the biggest single win is not allocating, which means `MergeInto` where the semantics allow it.

**What about memory?**

The pure merge needs both inputs plus the full result live simultaneously — roughly 2× the result. Per node the overhead is the object header, the key string and a `Dictionary` instance, and **the dictionary is the expensive part**: an empty `Dictionary<string, MetaNode>` is around 80 bytes, which on a tree of mostly-leaf nodes can exceed the data. Allocating it lazily, only when a node actually gains a child, is a large and easy saving.

Beyond that: pool and reuse buffers rather than allocating per node, keep allocations under the 85 KB Large Object Heap threshold, and if the trees are genuinely huge, consider a flattened representation — arrays of nodes indexed by integer rather than object references — which removes the per-object overhead entirely and is much less pleasant to work with.

*Trade-off:* Lazy dictionaries save a lot and add a null check on every access. A flattened array representation saves the most and costs readability and every existing traversal. `MergeInto` halves peak memory and gives up the concurrency properties. These are the same trade seen from three directions, and the right answer depends on whether the trees are held long-term or merged once and discarded.

**Level 1 — Correctness**

- *What are the edge cases — empty, duplicates, missing values, invalid input?* — Names them and says what the code does for each

**Level 2 — Complexity**

- *Time and space complexity? Can it be improved? What happens as N grows?* — States both, names the bottleneck

learn.title: 17 · Reference solution

designClaim: recurse key by key: build a new node whose value is the sum, union the children by key, and copy branches present on one side — never returning a node or a Children dictionary that belongs to an input
